facts.text: A Moravian mission station opened in April 1769 on East Hickory’s eastern Allegheny River bank, serving the Munsee Lenape until it closed in 1770.
Indigenous travelers crossed the Allegheny near East Hickory each spring to Oil Creek, where they gathered natural oil, boiled maple sugar, and built bark canoes.
The Hickory Valley Railroad ran from East Hickory in the late 1800s, linking local logging camps to wider markets.
Forest County, which contains East Hickory, was formed on April 11 1848 from Jefferson County and expanded in 1866 to include parts of Venango County.
East Hickory sits at 41°35′02″N 79°24′06″W, 1,079 feet above sea level, overlooking the Allegheny River.
After a Seneca famine in 1792, the Cornplanter band held annual squaw dances in East Hickory in 1806, drawing intertribal guests until a violent incident disrupted the event.
